findings.detail: The savings are being delivered through the transformation programme and service-led efficiencies. The budgeted growth was allocated mainly to adults and children's social care, education and housing, where costs have risen year on year.
findings.matters: Savings and growth of almost the same size show how much of the budget gap a council is closing through efficiency, which finance directors compare across councils.
findings.figures: £13.3m planned savings; £12.9m budgeted growth
findings.quote: included £13.3m of planned savings and £12.9m of budgeted growth.

findings.paper_title: Audit & Governance - Review of Savings Delivery 20261022
findings.headline: Paper names winter social care demand and a small rise in high-cost care packages as risks to the forecast
findings.detail: The paper says the forecast includes some allowance for future demand changes but that actual demand could exceed it. It identifies adults' and children's social care, education and housing as the highest financial risk areas.
findings.matters: A stated sensitivity to a small change in high-cost care numbers gives finance officers elsewhere a specific risk to test in their own people-services forecasts.
findings.figures: Not given
findings.quote: a small increase in the number of high cost care packages in social care could significantly impact the forecast spend.

findings.paper_title: Audit & Governance - Review of Savings Delivery 20261022

findings.matters: A forecast underspend at Q1 that is offset by named overspends is the position a finance director would test against their own directorate forecasts, and a lender would read as the council currently staying within its revenue budget.
findings.figures: £0.6m forecast underspend
findings.quote: Overall the Council is forecasting a £0.6m underspend, which is due to underspends and overachievement of savings in the People services

For years 2030/31 onwards, if transformation savings have not been locked in, the council faces a budget gap.
findings.matters: The council is using a temporary statutory power to offset structural budget pressures. When the power expires, if transformation savings haven't taken hold across the organisation, the council faces an immediate and potentially large budget gap that must be closed through service cuts, redundancies, or reserves.

findings.headline: Long-term financial performance depends on rents remaining affordable while operating costs inflate faster than rental income growth.
findings.detail: Rents on LAHF-funded acquisitions are capped at Local Housing Allowance (LHA), which historically has not increased at the same pace as inflation. The plan assumes LHA is frozen until 2027/28, then increases only 1% less than inflation. If LHA is frozen longer-term it could have material impact on SLL's financial performance. Section 12.4 notes that an increase in inflation would mean rents fall below operating costs since they are contractually constrained by LHA limits.
findings.matters: The council's housing company is exposed to a structural mismatch: operating costs will inflate faster than the capped rental income it can charge. Government policy on LHA uprating is outside the company's control and could force either subsidy dependence or reduction in service levels.
findings.figures: LHA assumed frozen until 2027/28, then rising 1% less than inflation annually
findings.quote: Historically, LHA has not always increased at the same pace as inflation. The base assumption of the plan is that LHA is frozen until 2027/28, from which point its average annual increase is 1% less than inflation. If it is frozen in the longer term it could start to have a material impact on SLLs financial performance.

news_drafts.headline: Sutton's schools grant deficit stands at £21.48m, with 90% of the historic deficit to be met by grant
news_drafts.lead:
Sutton Council has a £21.48m deficit on its dedicated schools grant (DSG), the government grant that funds schools. A DSG deficit is an overspend on that grant, usually on support for children with special needs. The figure is in the corporate risk register that the Audit and Governance Committee reviewed on 22 October 2026.

Government grant equal to 90% of the historic deficit will follow once the council's action plan is agreed with the Department for Education (DfE). The council has submitted its proposed plan and is awaiting confirmation of the approval process and the timing of the grant. It will fund the remaining 10%. It has put £1.64m from 2025/26 underspends into a deficit repayment reserve, money set aside for that purpose, and budgets a further £0.5m a year in its medium-term financial plan.

The statutory override, a temporary government rule that lets councils keep a schools-funding deficit off their main balance sheet, ends at the end of 2027/28. The paper says responsibility for any deficits incurred after that will sit with the DfE. It says it is currently unknown how deficits accumulated in 2026/27 and 2027/28 will be funded, though a similar mechanism to the 90% grant is assumed.

news_drafts.headline: Sutton forecasts £13.80m schools grant overspend for 2026/27, taking accumulated deficit to £35.28m
news_drafts.lead:
Sutton forecasts an overspend of £13.80m on its dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) for 2026/27, which would take the accumulated deficit on the grant to £35.28m at the year-end. The figure adds to £21.48m carried forward from 2025/26. The Strategy and Resources Committee noted the forecast on 5 October 2026, and its minute sets out no funding solution for the balance.

Of the overspend, £13.71m is in high needs, the part of the grant for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND). The quarter 1 report attributes it to sustained national and local growth in demand for statutory SEND support, with active Education, Health and Care Plans reaching 2,789 in June 2026. It says neither the "Experts at Hand" initiative nor the SEND Reform Plan sent to the Department for Education in June 2026 is expected to reduce spending materially this year.

The government's High Needs Stability Grant will cover 90% of historic deficits. The remaining 10% must be met locally when the statutory override, a temporary rule keeping such deficits off the council's main accounts, ends. The report gives that share as £2.15m in one place and about £5.5m by 2027/28 in another. A reserve of £1.64m is held. A £2m contribution and £0.58m in each of 2026/27, 2027/28 and 2028/29 would take it to £5.38m. Carrying the balance costs about £1m a year in lost interest or borrowing expenses, the report says.

news_drafts.headline: Sutton's schools-funding deficit forecast to reach £35.6m, with the council responsible for at least £3.6m
news_drafts.lead:
Sutton Council's deficit on the dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) is forecast to rise from £21.6m to £35.6m, according to the medium-term financial strategy (the council's financial plan for the next three to five years) put to its Strategy and Resources Committee on 5 October. The extra £14m is forecast growth on the £21.6m accumulated so far.

The government has committed to fund 90% of accumulated deficits on high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. That leaves Sutton responsible for the remaining 10%, which the strategy puts at a minimum of £3.6m. The papers give the government's share as up to about £32m.

The council has budgeted to set money aside against its share. It plans a £0.5m contribution to its dedicated schools grant reserve in 2027/28, followed by a further £2m in 2028/29. The strategy covers the years 2026 to 2030.
